summary: I read world_mind.py and actor_mind.py in full, traced the intention -> world -> journal path in trajectory.py, and cross-referenced all 178 committed events in the 21 runs under artifacts/simulations_v3 and artifacts/matched_pairs against the world_judgments trigger that produced each one, plus the raw event-review verdicts in every ledger. The actor half is genuinely sound: an actor cannot author reality. There are exactly two journal.commit call-sites (trajectory.py:859, adapter.py:94), every one of the 178 committed events carries source 'starting_event[i]' or 'world_call:cN', private_updates reach only that actor's own memory list, and an actor cannot schedule a wake for anyone but themselves. The world half fails. The world writes people's decisions into committed history in at least five separate runs -- reading, opening, replying, skipping, closing, typing, pressing Enter -- on triggers that were nobody's intention, and two of the six YES answers cite or causally depend on exactly such an event. Worse, on the occasions the event review does catch it, trajectory.py:290 hands the turn to the wrong person, because it uses the event's audience list as the identity of the decider.

findings.title: The world authors people's decisions as committed history, including events the terminal answer rests on
findings.evidence: artifacts/simulations_v3/case2_negotiation journal e721 (world_call:c377, trigger 'pending_progression'): "Dmitri opens the messaging app and reads the unread messages from Priya: the follow-up asking if he saw her 1100 offer, and the acceptance of 1150." -- and terminal_result.json for that run cites e721 in its YES. artifacts/matched_pairs/c1_against_stereotype e252 (world_call:c139, 'pending_progression'): "The vendor support representative finishes typing the pairing code into the support system and presses Enter", whose only consequence e268 is cited in that run's YES; also e78, e129, e242. artifacts/matched_pairs/a1_responsive e45 (world_call:c20, 'event_consequence'): "Marcus Bell reads Dana Whitfield's message...". artifacts/matched_pairs/b1_okafor_herrera__r2 e32 (world_call:c2, trigger 'starting_event', i.e. before Aisha had ever taken a turn): "Aisha opens the email from Tomas Herrera and reads the attached lease document", and e29: "...fully read and understood by her". artifacts/matched_pairs/a2_unresponsive__r3 e117/e149/e192 ('pending_progression'/'event_consequence'): "Marcus continues working through his inbox, skipping over Dana's unread emails without opening them", "Marcus closes his email client for the day", "Marcus closes his email client without opening Dana's messages". Every one of these was PASSed by the event review (ledger semantic.event_review c378, c139, c21, c3, c9, c61, c82, c108) -- c378's stated reason is "Dmitri has noticed the messages and now chooses to open and read them", i.e. the reviewer names it as a choice and passes it anyway.
findings.why_it_matters: world_mind.py:60-68 states the rule verbatim -- "Never write that someone opens, reads, answers, agrees, refuses, accepts, decides, goes, buys, signs, or acts on something" -- and world_mind.py:354-362 makes exactly those verbs the definition of ACTOR_TURN_REQUIRED. The only enforcement is that prompt plus an LLM reviewer, and there is no code-level guard anywhere. In practice the reviewer passes them, so the governing rule 'LLMs write social meaning, but only people decide what people do' is not held by anything. The consequence is not cosmetic: case2's YES cites a world-invented act of reading, and c1's YES rests on e268 whose sole cause is a world-invented keypress, so the answers of those runs are partly the world's decisions rather than the actors'.
findings.suggested_fix: Thread the acting actor id into _event_review and refuse to commit any event whose subject is an actor other than the one whose intention (or own follow_up chain) triggered it, treating it as ACTOR_TURN_REQUIRED for that person rather than relying on the reviewer to notice.

findings.title: When the review does catch a world-written choice, the turn is handed to the wrong person and the decision is silently dropped
findings.evidence: trajectory.py:290-292: `who = [a for a in envelope["for"] if journal.observed_by(a)] or list(envelope["for"])` then `handed_to: who[0]` / `actor_step(who[0], ...)`. But world_mind.py:149-152 documents `for` as "the actor ids the event or its information becomes AVAILABLE to -- which is usually the person it is heading TOWARDS, not the person who set it in motion". Live consequences, from the ledgers: artifacts/matched_pairs/a1_responsive world_call c29 -- rejected event "Marcus Bell replies to Dana Whitfield that the hall is confirmed for the 14th", review reason "Replying is an action Marcus Bell chooses to take", handed_to = dana_whitfield. artifacts/matched_pairs/c1_against_stereotype c13 -- rejected event "The vendor support representative greets Ethel and asks how they can assist", review reason "...the vendor support representative deciding to greet...", handed_to = ethel_pomeroy. Same run c162 -- rejected event "The vendor support representative tells Ethel that the pairing code was accepted...", handed_to = ethel_pomeroy. Three of the eight live hand-offs went to somebody other than the person whose choice had been written.
findings.why_it_matters: The whole point of the ACTOR_TURN_REQUIRED verdict is to return a usurped decision to its owner. Instead the recipient of the information is consulted, the actual decider is never asked at that moment, and the world's answer is discarded with nothing put in its place -- so the decision the review correctly protected simply does not happen. The accompanying filter is also inert: `journal.observed_by(a)` returns every event a has ever observed, so its truthiness means only 'has this person ever observed anything', not the comment's claim at trajectory.py:289-291 that 'they have the observation that would let them choose'.
findings.suggested_fix: Have the world (or the reviewer) name the actor whose choice the rejected event contained, validate that id in code, and hand the turn to that actor rather than to `envelope["for"][0]`.

findings.title: The ACTOR_TURN_REQUIRED -> PASS override is blind to whose choice was written
findings.evidence: trajectory.py:401-410 converts the verdict to PASS whenever `trigger_kind == "actor_intention"`, with no check that the person acting in the event is the person whose intention triggered it; _event_review is not even given the actor id. That the runtime produces cross-actor events on actor_intention triggers is demonstrated live: artifacts/matched_pairs/c1_against_stereotype e105 (world_call:c56) has trigger "ethel_pomeroy attempts: Wait for the support representative's instructions and follow them to complete the pairing step" and commits "The vendor support representative begins explaining the pairing step to Ethel..."; e295 (world_call:c166) has trigger "ethel_pomeroy attempts: Wait for the vendor support representative to confirm..." and commits "The vendor support representative tells Ethel that the pairing code has been accepted and the terminal is now paired successfully." vendor_support_representative is a full actor with its own private_context and nine turns of its own. The override fired 10 times across the runs and in all 10 the actor happened to match, so the hole has not yet been observed to fire wrongly; tests/test_semantic_runtime.py:1842 only exercises the same-actor case.
findings.why_it_matters: One reviewer verdict away from the runtime committing actor B's decision as fact because actor A attempted something -- and c1 shows the world already writes exactly that shape of event. Combined with finding 1, the same-actor exemption is the only thing keeping the override defensible, and nothing in the code checks it.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass the triggering actor id into _event_review and apply the override only when the event's subject is that same actor.

findings.title: The pending_progression trigger hands the world one named person's private motivation and asks it to say what that person does
findings.evidence: trajectory.py:627-641 and 909-918 call world_step(trigger_kind="pending_progression", actor_id=aid, ...), and trajectory.py:233-236 puts that actor's compiler-written private_context into the world prompt. The live prompt for artifacts/matched_pairs/a2_unresponsive__r3 world call c81 reads: "THE PERSON THIS CONCERNS marcus_bell / their circumstances (background for your judgment only, never to be repeated in an event): Marcus has not answered Dana's last four messages. He told a colleague in August that he is avoiding Dana since the argument about the invoices..." followed by "What concretely becomes of them next?". The answer committed as e149 was "Marcus closes his email client for the day, leaving Dana's messages unread in his inbox." Six of the nine committed events in that run are Marcus's conduct written this way.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the structural source of most of finding 1. Being told a person's private motive and then asked what becomes of a thing 'for them' is an invitation to enact that motive; the guard 'never to be repeated in an event' forbids quotation, not enactment. The run in question is a matched-pair arm whose entire purpose is to test whether behaviour tracks evidence, and its behaviour was produced by the world reading the evidence rather than by the person acting on it. (Marcus's own 19 turns happened to agree, so nothing contradicts, but the specifics were the world's.)
findings.suggested_fix: Narrow the pending_progression question to attention only -- whether the item moves, arrives or reaches awareness -- and refuse any returned event in which the named person does something other than notice.

findings.title: The event-review artifact records the post-override verdict, so the overrides are invisible to an auditor
findings.evidence: trajectory.py:394-399 writes the raw verdict to the ledger via OP_EVENT_REVIEW, but trajectory.py:411-413 calls note("event_review", **verdict) after the override at 401-410, and trace.py:82-83 builds event_quality_reviews.jsonl from those notes. Verified in artifacts/matched_pairs/a1_responsive: ledger call c28 records verdict ACTOR_TURN_REQUIRED, event_quality_reviews.jsonl records the same call as PASS. All 10 live overrides are similarly absent from the review artifact.
findings.why_it_matters: The artifact a reader inspects to check whether the world ever put a decision in somebody's mouth is exactly the artifact from which those cases have been removed. It makes the mechanism in finding 3 unauditable without reading the ledger.
findings.suggested_fix: Record both the raw verdict and the override in the trace note, e.g. verdict=PASS with overridden_from=ACTOR_TURN_REQUIRED.

findings.title: Starting events bypass the per-person attention rule, inconsistently with identical events scheduled later
findings.evidence: adapter.py:86-97 hardcodes "observed": True for the whole visible_to audience, and trajectory.py:813-821 commits such an event without passing it through the group split. The split at trajectory.py:854-858 only applies on the K_EVENT path, so an identical starting event whose time is after the start (adapter.py:98-102 schedules it as K_EVENT) would instead be forced to observed=False for everyone. Live: artifacts/simulations_v3/case2_negotiation e11 is the only committed event in all 21 runs with observed=True and more than one actor in "for" (['priya_raghavan','dmitri_sokolov']).
findings.why_it_matters: The same compiler declaration is honoured or silently overridden depending only on whether the event's time equals the start instant. It is defensible for a scene premise to be shared, but it should be one rule, not two.
findings.suggested_fix: Apply the same per-person rule to both starting-event paths, or exempt compiler-declared starting events from the split explicitly and identically in both.
